title: Where it grows
subtitle: Cool climates around the world
objectives: Explain why it needs a cool climate

steps.title: Cool climates
steps.body: Pinot Noir needs a cool climate. In heat, it ripens too fast, losing its delicate aromas and acidity and turning jammy. A long, cool season builds complexity. Its main homes are Burgundy, Champagne, Germany, Oregon, California's coast, New Zealand, Chile's coast, Australia's Victoria and Tasmania.

steps.title: Clones
steps.body: Pinot Noir mutates easily, so there are hundreds of clones, each with different berry size, yield and flavour. Dijon clones, like 115, 667 and 777, developed in Burgundy, spread worldwide from the 1980s. California's Pommard and Wädenswil clones are also widely planted. Many growers plant several clones for complexity.

steps.prompt: What happens to Pinot Noir in a hot climate?
options: It ripens too fast, losing aroma and turning jammy
steps.explanation: Heat speeds ripening, losing the delicacy Pinot is prized for.

steps.title: Mutations
steps.body: Pinot Noir is the parent or ancestor of many grapes. Pinot Gris and Pinot Blanc are colour mutations; Meunier is another mutation. Crossed with Gouais Blanc, it gave Chardonnay, Gamay, Aligoté and Melon. That makes it one of the most important grapes in the history of wine.

steps.prompt: Which grapes are mutations of Pinot Noir?

steps.title: What you learned
points: Pinot Noir needs a cool climate
Hundreds of clones, like the Dijon clones, exist
It's the ancestor of Chardonnay, Gamay and others
